IB Computer Science

A1.2 Data Representation & Logic

Topic A1: Computer Fundamentals | From Meaning → Bits

Retrieval Practice

Recall A1.1 (Computer Hardware) before we move on.

  1. Which register stores the address of the next instruction?
  2. Which bus carries memory addresses from CPU to RAM?
  3. What is the difference between a cache hit and a cache miss?

Press Down for answers

Answer 1

Which register stores the address of the next instruction?

Program Counter (PC) — it points to the next instruction to fetch.

Answer 2

Which bus carries memory addresses from CPU to RAM?

Address bus — it carries the location (not the data itself).

Answer 3

What is the difference between a cache hit and a cache miss?

Hit: data is found in cache (fast). Miss: data must be fetched from slower memory (stall).

The Big Question

🤔 A photo, a song, and your password look totally different.

So how can a computer store them all using the same memory?

❌ Misconception: "Computers store images as tiny pictures and sound as tiny waves."

In memory, everything must be reduced to patterns of 0s and 1s.

✅ Key idea: bits only have meaning because we agree on an encoding rule.

Different data types use different representations: numbers, characters, samples, pixels…

Why binary?

Why did modern computing "choose" base‑2 instead of base‑10?

Hardware is built from switches (transistors) with two stable states: on/off.

Two-state systems are robust against electrical noise.

1 byte = 8 bits → 256 possible patterns (0–255 for unsigned integers).

Human-friendly bases

Denary is convenient for humans.

Hexadecimal is convenient for humans reading binary (4 bits per hex digit).

Base Conversions

How do we move between binary, denary, and hex without guessing?

Binary → denary uses place values (powers of 2).

Denary → binary uses repeated division by 2 (remainders).

Binary ↔ hex groups bits into 4‑bit nibbles.

Press Down for worked methods

Binary → Denary (Place Values)

Example: 01102

Place values: 8, 4, 2, 1

0×8 + 1×4 + 1×2 + 0×1 = 610

Denary → Binary (Divide by 2)

Example: 1310

Divide by 2 and record remainders: 13→6 r1, 6→3 r0, 3→1 r1, 1→0 r1

Read remainders bottom‑to‑top: 11012

Binary ↔ Hex (4-bit Groups)

Example: 1010 11112

1010 = A, 1111 = F

So 1010 11112 = AF16

Why hex is useful: one hex digit exactly represents 4 bits, so long binary patterns become readable.

🧠 Quick Check

What denary value is 100100002?

144 — because 128 + 16 = 144.

Representing Text

When you press A, how does the computer know which letter you meant?

ASCII maps characters to numbers (codes).

Unicode extends this idea to support global writing systems and symbols.

Key idea: text is stored as numeric codes in binary.

Why Unicode matters

ASCII struggles with non‑English alphabets and emoji.

Unicode provides code points for many scripts (Latin, Arabic, Chinese…).

Representing Images

Why does a "higher quality" image usually mean a larger file?

A bitmap image is a grid of pixels.

Resolution increases the number of pixels.

Colour depth increases the number of bits per pixel.

Uncompressed size: width × height × colour depth (bits).

Compression

Lossless: exact original restored (e.g., PNG).

Lossy: trades quality for size (e.g., JPEG).

Quick Check

🧠 Quick Check

If you double both width and height, what happens to the number of pixels?

It becomes 4× larger (area scales with width × height).

Representing Sound (Sampling)

How can a continuous sound wave become discrete binary data?

Sampling rate measures how often we take a sample.

Bit depth controls precision (quantisation levels).

Uncompressed size: sampling rate × bit depth × duration × channels.

Intuition

Higher sampling rate captures higher frequencies.

Higher bit depth reduces quantisation error (less "stepping").

Representing Video

Why is raw video enormous — and why is compression essential?

Video is a sequence of images (frames) + audio.

High resolution × high frame rate × high colour depth → massive data rates.

Two compression ideas

Spatial: compress within one frame (similar pixels).

Temporal: compress across frames (only changes are stored).

🔗 Connection to A2: streaming video works because data is split into packets and delivered over networks with buffering and error control.

Logic Gates

How can hardware "decide" between two actions using only 0 and 1?

Logic gates implement Boolean operations in hardware.

Inputs/outputs are binary: 1 (true) or 0 (false).

Common gates: AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR.

Why gates matter

They are the basis of adders, comparators, memory, and CPU control logic.

At scale, "software" becomes electrical decisions through gate networks.

Truth Tables & Logic Diagrams

How do we prove a logic circuit is correct?

A truth table lists all input combinations and outputs.

A logic diagram visualises gates wired together.

Press Down for an example

Example: Y = A AND (NOT B)

ABNOT BY
0010
0100
1011
1100

Interpretation: the output is 1 only when A is 1 and B is 0.

🧠 Quick Check

If A=1 and B=1, what is Y = A AND (NOT B)?

0 — because NOT B = 0, and 1 AND 0 = 0.

HL Karnaugh Maps (K‑Maps)

How can we simplify Boolean expressions without "guessing"?

A Karnaugh map groups 1s to remove redundant variables.

Headings use Gray code so adjacent cells differ by one bit.

What you gain

Simpler circuits: fewer gates → lower cost, lower delay, fewer failure points.

Cleaner expressions: easier to analyse and implement.

Misconception Check

A. Hexadecimal is "how the computer stores data internally".

B. Increasing sampling rate increases uncompressed audio file size.

C. Lossless compression always makes a file smaller.

D. A truth table can be used to verify a logic circuit.

Press Down for answers

Answers

A: False. Computers store in binary; hex is a human-friendly shorthand.

B: True. More samples per second = more data (before compression).

C: False. Some data is already close to random/uncompressible.

D: True. It exhaustively checks all input combinations.

Key Takeaways

  • All data is stored as binary, but meaning comes from representation rules.
  • We convert between binary, denary, and hex using systematic methods.
  • Text, images, audio, and video rely on encoding + (often) compression.
  • Digital circuits use logic gates, verified by truth tables.
  • HL K‑maps simplify Boolean expressions using Gray-code adjacency.
